strengths.title: Coherent mechanism combining adversarial and orthogonality losses
strengths.description: The model integrates multi-class adversarial minimax with a Frobenius orthogonality penalty into a shared-private LSTM architecture to target contamination and redundancy explicitly.
evidence: Clear definitions in §4.2 (LAdv Eq.13) and §4.3 (Ldiff Eq.14) and combined loss in §4.4 (Eq.15).
References to prior work (Ajakan et al. 2014; Bousmalis et al. 2016; Ganin & Lempitsky 2015) provide conceptual grounding.

strengths.title: Extensive empirical scope across many tasks
strengths.description: Evaluation covers 16 distinct sentiment/text-classification datasets, demonstrating empirical breadth uncommon in single-paper MTL studies.
evidence: Table 1 dataset statistics and Tables 2–3 reporting per-task results across all 16 datasets.

strengths.title: Practical transfer experiment design
strengths.description: The frozen shared-layer transfer (single- and bi-channel) is a practical demonstration of reusing learned shared extractors for new tasks.
evidence: §5.5 describes transfer experiments; Table 3 reports transfer performance across tasks.

concerns.title: No multiple-run statistics or significance testing
concerns.description: Quantitative results (Tables 2 and 3) are reported as single-run point estimates with no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests; this obscures whether reported gains are robust to random initialization and training noise.
evidence: Tables 2–3 list single numbers per method/task and the text lacks mentions of multiple seeds or tests.
Shared analysis and prior reviewers flagged absence of variance reporting and statistical testing.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run each experimental condition (especially key comparisons SP-MTL vs ASP-MTL and transfer settings) with multiple random seeds (≥5) and report mean±std and statistical tests (e.g., paired t-test or Wilcoxon) on per-task and average metrics.

concerns.title: No direct operationalization of 'shared purity' or task-identifiability
concerns.description: Central claim that adversarial training purifies shared features is not directly measured; manuscript lacks diagnostics such as held-out discriminator accuracy pre/post training, mutual information estimates, or task-classification from shared representations.
evidence: §4.2 motivates adversarial loss by domain-adaptation theory but provides no empirical measurement of task-identifiability reduction.
Shared analysis recommends measuring discriminator accuracy on held-out features; paper does not present this.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Train separate held-out task-discriminators on frozen shared representations from models with/without adversarial loss to quantify task-identifiability reductions; report the discriminator accuracy and correlate with transfer/downstream performance.

concerns.title: Orthogonality metric enforces only linear decorrelation
concerns.description: The Frobenius penalty penalizes linear correlations between shared and private matrix outputs but may not remove nonlinear redundancy; no nonlinear similarity or mutual information measures are provided.
evidence: §4.3 uses ||S_k^T H_k||_F^2 and cites Bousmalis et al. (2016); reviewers note this penalizes linear overlap.
No empirical analysis of nonlinear redundancy (e.g., CKA, HSIC, mutual information) is present.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Complement Ldiff with nonlinear similarity diagnostics (e.g., centered kernel alignment, HSIC, or mutual information estimators) between shared and private representations and report whether orthogonality reduces these measures; consider augmenting loss if nonlinear redundancy persists.

concerns.title: Semi-supervised claim not empirically demonstrated
concerns.description: Although LAdv only depends on input x and could use unlabeled data, no semi-supervised experiments using additional unlabeled corpora are shown to validate this capability.
evidence: §4.2 claims LAdv 'does not require the corresponding label y, which makes it possible to combine our model with semi-supervised learning', but §5 contains no such experiments.
Dataset table includes an 'Unlab.' column but their use is not described in experiments.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run a controlled semi-supervised experiment: add unlabeled data to adversarial loss only (keeping task losses on labeled data) and report performance changes compared to no-unlabeled and to SP-MTL; describe unlabeled data selection and sizes.

concerns.title: Baseline tuning and implementation parity under-specified
concerns.description: Comparisons to baselines (MT-CNN, MT-DNN, FS-MTL, SP-MTL) may be affected by differing hyperparameter searches, embedding initializations, or model capacities; the manuscript does not document tuning budgets or whether architectures were capacity-matched.
evidence: §5.2 lists baselines but provides limited tuning details; §5.3 describes grid for proposed model only.
Shared analysis notes potential confound from baseline reimplementation differences.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide detailed baseline configs (embedding dims, hidden sizes, number of params), reproduce baselines with matched capacities and comparable tuning budgets, or cite exact public implementations and hyperparameters used.

concerns.title: Interpretability evidence anecdotal and limited-scale
concerns.description: Neuron activation visualizations and token-pattern lists are useful but drawn from few examples; claims about systematic specialization lack population-level statistics.
evidence: §5.6 presents one sentence example and Table 4 listing patterns for two tasks; no aggregate measures of neuron specialization are reported.
Shared analysis recommends measures such as fraction of specialized neurons or overlap of top-k tokens.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute aggregate interpretability metrics (e.g., percent overlap of top-k activating tokens between shared/private units, entropy of neuron activations across tasks, CKA between shared/private matrices) and report distributions across units/datasets.

comparable_works.relevance: Precedent for using orthogonality/Frobenius penalty to separate shared and private representations in domain adaptation; conceptual closest prior work.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: uses orthogonality loss to separate latent spaces and adversarial ideas for invariance. Difference: Bousmalis focused on domain separation (visual) and binary domain adversarial objectives; this paper extends adversarial idea to multi-class tasks and LSTM text models.
comparable_works.source_trace: Cited in manuscript (§4.3) and shared retrieval (Bousmalis et al., 2016).

comparable_works.relevance: Provides optimization technique (gradient reversal) to implement adversarial feature learning used here.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: minimax via gradient reversal to learn domain-invariant features. Difference: original primarily binary domain adaptation; current work adapts to multi-class task discriminator and MTL setting.
comparable_works.source_trace: Cited in manuscript (§4.4) and in shared references.

comparable_works.relevance: Theoretical connection between adversarial loss and distributional divergence used as justification for adversarial objective producing invariant features.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: connects adversarial loss to H-divergence and transferability arguments. Difference: Ajakan focuses on domain adaptation; manuscript applies to multi-task settings.
comparable_works.source_trace: Cited in §4.1 of the manuscript.

comparable_works.relevance: Classic multi-task neural approach (MT-CNN) used as baseline and conceptual predecessor for shared parameter sharing.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Difference: CNN-based and earlier sharing approaches; ASP-MTL proposes explicit separation and adversarial loss not present in original works.
comparable_works.source_trace: Cited in §5.2 as MT-CNN baseline.

uncertainty_flags: Reported numeric gains are single-run results; variance across random seeds unknown.
'Purity' claim is not operationalized with direct diagnostics; reliance on downstream accuracy and anecdotal visualizations is indirect.
Orthogonality penalty measures linear correlations only; nonlinear redundancy may persist undetected.
Semi-supervised/unlabeled-data claims are theoretical with no empirical validation here.
Baseline implementation/tuning parity is under-documented, creating potential confound for performance claims.
alternative_interpretations: The observed improvements could stem partly from regularization effects of the additional loss terms (LAdv and Ldiff) rather than semantic purification; regularization could reduce overfitting and improve generalization without achieving true task-invariance.
Optimization dynamics of gradient reversal can alter feature magnitudes and gradient flows, producing better-trained models for this dataset suite independent of the purity/disjointness rationale.
Differences in hyperparameter tuning (e.g., more careful tuning for ASP-MTL) or slight architecture/capacity mismatches between baselines and proposed model could account for some gains.
A frozen shared layer improving held-out tasks may primarily provide stronger pretraining (initialization) than 'off-the-shelf' disentangled features; fine-tuning results could differ.
transparency_notes: The manuscript provides equations for losses and a brief hyperparameter grid, but lacks details about random seeds, number of runs, early stopping rules, exact optimizer settings (beyond learning rate), and precise baseline hyperparameters.
Tables present only single-run error rates; code or configuration files are not referenced for reproducibility.
Dataset partitioning is described as random splits (70/20/10) but no seed or split files are provided; this can affect comparability.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: Although the combination of multi-class adversarial discriminator and orthogonality is an incremental composition of prior techniques, sparse direct analogs in text-LSTM multi-task literature make it a defensible engineering novelty; however, being novel does not guarantee that the empirical claims are valid without stronger diagnostics and robustness checks.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If discriminator capacity and optimization are adequate and held-out discriminator accuracy on shared features drops substantially post-training, then adversarial loss likely produced meaningful task-invariance and transfer gains.

If orthogonality loss reduces both linear and nonlinear redundancy (measured via CKA/HSIC/mutual information) across multiple runs, then combined ASP-MTL plausibly enforces disjoint encodings and explains accuracy improvements.
If multi-seed experiments show consistent average improvements with small variance and statistical significance, then reported single-run gains generalize reliably.
If semi-supervised experiments using extra unlabeled sentences improve the adversarial objective and downstream task accuracy, then the claim about leveraging unlabeled data is empirically supported.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Combines established elements (adversarial domain-style loss, orthogonality penalty, shared-private architecture) into an LSTM-based MTL setting and extends binary adversarial training to multi-class; assembly is coherent but not a radical new paradigm.
evidence: Citations to Ganin & Lempitsky (2015), Bousmalis et al. (2016) show close antecedents; manuscript extends them to multi-class MTL and LSTM.
uncertainty_flags: Relative novelty depends on how many prior works already applied adversarial+orthogonality to multi-task NLP specifically; retrieved literature shows domain-adaptation analogs but fewer direct text-LSTM MTL precedents.

novelty_lenses.rationale: While empirical gains across many small sentiment datasets and a frozen-transfer demonstration suggest practical value, lack of robust statistical validation and direct diagnostics limits the claim that this method will systematically replace prior MTL practices across domains.
evidence: Average error improvements in Tables 2–3 are sizable but single-run; transfer results show frozen shared layer helps on average.
uncertainty_flags: Reproducibility and generality across larger or different-domain datasets (beyond small sentiment corpora) remain untested.

confidence_interval.rationale: I have high confidence in the manuscript's claims about the proposed architecture and that reported single-run numbers support plausibility of improvements, but substantial uncertainty remains because of missing multiple-run statistics, lack of direct diagnostics for key mechanistic claims (purity/disjointness), and under-specified baseline parity. If requested robustness checks (multi-seed runs, held-out discriminator measurements, nonlinear redundancy metrics, semi-supervised experiments) were performed and confirm current findings, confidence would move toward the upper bound.

consensus_findings: The paper presents a coherent, implementable combination of a multi-class adversarial task discriminator and a Frobenius-norm orthogonality penalty within a shared-private LSTM MTL architecture (ASP-MTL).

Empirical evaluation covers a broad set of 16 sentiment/text-classification datasets and includes a practical frozen-shared-layer transfer protocol (single- and bi-channel) — providing useful empirical breadth.
Reported single-run results show that ASP-MTL yields lower error rates (per the provided tables) relative to the listed single-task and multi-task baselines on average.

Key methodological/reporting gaps are consistently noted: quantitative results are presented as single point estimates without multiple-run variance or statistical testing; mechanistic claims (that adversarial training makes the shared space 'purer' and that the Frobenius orthogonality enforces semantic disjointness) lack direct, quantitative diagnostics.
Interpretability evidence (neuron visualizations / token-pattern lists) is informative but limited and anecdotal; reviewers request population-level statistics to support representativeness.

Baseline implementation/tuning parity and reproducibility details (code, seeds, full baseline hyperparameter searches, optimizer/training protocols, dataset splits) are insufficiently documented to rule out implementation or tuning confounds.
disagreements: Degree of novelty: some reviewers treat the contribution as an expected, useful incremental engineering synthesis of existing ideas (adversarial invariance + orthogonality + shared-private MTL), while others view the specific multi-class adversarial + frozen-transfer framing as a conceptually encouraging or modestly original signal. (Preserved controlled disagreement: novelty is seen as incremental by several reviewers but as an interesting compositional idea by others.)

Interpretation of empirical gains: reviewers differ on whether the reported average improvements (single-run) are plausibly meaningful as-is (some find the breadth suggestive) versus likely to be sensitive to tuning/random seeds and therefore requiring more robustness checks before stronger claims can be supported.

Assessment of orthogonality efficacy: some reviewers emphasize prior precedent (Bousmalis et al.) and see the Frobenius penalty as reasonable for linear decorrelation; others stress this is insufficient to claim semantic disjointness without nonlinear-similarity diagnostics.
uncertainty_hotspots: Purity operationalization: no held-out probe/discriminator accuracy or explicit task-identifiability metric is reported to demonstrate that shared representations actually lose task-specific signal while retaining useful shared information.

Orthogonality semantics: the Frobenius penalty enforces linear decorrelation but may leave nonlinear redundancy; absence of CKA/SVCCA/HSIC/mutual-information-style analyses leaves the semantic-disjointness claim underdetermined.
Statistical robustness: single-run point estimates (Tables 2/3) lack mean ± std or CIs and no per-task significance tests are reported; improvement magnitudes are therefore epistemically uncertain.

Baseline parity and tuning: limited documentation of baseline architectures, parameter counts, and tuning budgets creates uncertainty whether observed gains reflect architectural merit or differential tuning/implementation.

Semi-supervised claim: the statement that LAdv 'allows unlabeled data' is not empirically tested in the manuscript; hence practical utility of multi-class adversarial extension for semi-supervised learning is speculative here.

Minimax training dynamics: no training curves, discriminator-capacity ablations, or stability analyses are provided; sensitivity to adversarial strength λ, discriminator size, and gradient reversal behavior is unclear.

Transfer regime generality: transfer experiments evaluate frozen shared-layer reuse only; absence of fine-tuning comparisons limits conclusions about practical transfer strategies and when freezing is preferred.
model_diversity_effects: Structure-analyst emphasis produced a clear logical decomposition of the causal chain (adversarial -> purity; orthogonality -> less redundancy; both -> performance/transfer) and highlighted internal argumentative gaps (lack of direct measures).

Methodology-auditor focus prioritized reproducibility and validity checks (multi-seed experiments, held-out probes, baseline parity), elevating concerns about single-run reporting and untested semi-supervised claims.

Novelty-assessor reviewers (incremental and disruptive lenses) produced controlled disagreement on originality: they placed the work relative to domain-adaptation and domain-separation precedents, yielding nuanced views that treat absence of close text-LSTM analogs as an innovation signal but not proof of broad impact.
Claim-verifier review reinforced evidence-first concerns and requested concrete diagnostics (CKA/MI/probing classifiers) and systematic ablations to validate causal links stated in the manuscript.

Together, the role diversity increased coverage of diagnostic and reproducibility checks requested, and preserved differing weightings of novelty vs rigor — producing a synthesis that stresses needed empirical probes without averaging away disagreements about contribution novelty.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Maintain central decision authority. If additional experiments/analyses are feasible within a reasonable revision cycle, ask authors to (1) provide multi-seed reruns (≥5 seeds) for core quantitative comparisons (ASP-MTL vs SP-MTL and strongest baselines) and report mean ± standard deviation and perform appropriate paired statistical tests for average and per-task metrics; (2) add direct diagnostics for the 'purity' claim by training held-out task discriminators (or probe classifiers) on frozen shared representations before/after adversarial training and reporting task-identifiability metrics; (3) quantify redundancy reduction beyond linear correlation via at least one nonlinear similarity measure (e.g., CKA or SVCCA) or mutual-information proxy between shared and private outputs and report how Ldiff affects these measures; (4) supply ablations isolating contributions of LAdv and LDiff across seeds and a sensitivity sweep for λ and γ, plus training curves (task loss, LAdv, LDiff, discriminator accuracy) to assess minimax stability; (5) document baseline implementations, hyperparameter grids, and parameter counts to ensure fair comparisons; (6) add at least one controlled semi-supervised experiment using unlabeled sentences in LAdv to empirically substantiate that claim; and (7) expand interpretability analyses from anecdotal examples to population-level statistics (e.g., fraction of specialized neurons, top-k token overlap). If space is limited, prioritize items (1)-(4) and baseline transparency. Use these expanded diagnostics as the central criteria for re-assessing the paper's empirical claims.
meta_review.author_guidance: To address reviewers' concerns and strengthen mechanistic and empirical claims, provide the following revisions and additional analyses: (a) Re-run the core experiments (Tables 2 and 3) across multiple random seeds (recommend ≥5) and report mean ± std and 95% CIs; include paired statistical tests (e.g., bootstrap or Wilcoxon) comparing ASP-MTL to SP-MTL and single-task baselines for average and per-task metrics. (b) Directly measure 'shared-space purity' by training independent held-out task-discriminators or probe classifiers on frozen shared representations from models trained with and without LAdv; report discriminator accuracy/AUC and correlate changes with transfer/performance gains. (c) Quantify redundancy reduction between shared and private encodings using one or more nonlinear similarity metrics (CKA/SVCCA/HSIC) and/or mutual information proxies; report distributions across tasks and seeds and ablate Ldiff. (d) Provide ablation experiments separating effects of adversarial loss and orthogonality loss (only-LAdv, only-LDiff, neither) across seeds and sweep λ and γ more broadly to show sensitivity and choose robust settings. (e) Release full implementation details for baselines (architectural sizes, embedding handling, optimizer settings, hyperparameter grids, number of tuning trials) and match parameter counts where possible; if public baseline implementations were used, cite versions and settings. (f) Add training diagnostics: per-epoch curves for task loss, LAdv, LDiff, and discriminator accuracy to demonstrate minimax convergence and stability; ablate discriminator capacity and gradient-reversal scaling where informative. (g) Include at least one semi-supervised experiment that injects unlabeled data into LAdv to empirically demonstrate (or qualify) claims about unlabeled-data utility. (h) Expand neuron-level analyses to population statistics (e.g., percent of neurons whose top-k activating tokens are unique to shared/private channels, activation entropy) to support interpretability claims. (i) Share code, random seeds, and exact dataset splits to enable reproducibility. If time/space is limited, prioritize (a)-(d) and baseline transparency (e), then add the remaining items as possible.
transparency_report: Missing or insufficiently reported items: number of independent runs / random seeds per reported point estimate (Tables 2/3 give single numbers only).
Baseline implementations: no detailed descriptions of competitor architectures' parameter counts, embedding handling, or hyperparameter search budgets — fairness of comparisons is under-documented.

Optimization/training details: absence of per-epoch training curves, discriminator architecture/capacity choices, early-stopping criteria, and minimax/gradient-reversal hyperparameters (e.g., schedule for reversal or scaling).
Dataset splits and seeds: dataset splitting is described generically (70/20/10) but exact splits or random seeds are not provided.
Code and artifacts: no repository or scripts for reproducing reported results, neuron-visualization pipelines, or transferred shared-layer artifacts are referenced.
Ablation/logging artifacts: LAdv-only and LDiff-only ablation statistics (across seeds) and held-out discriminator probe results are not reported.
Semi-supervised usage: although the Unlab. column appears in dataset table, no explicit experimental protocol or results using unlabeled data with LAdv are provided.
epistemic_limits: Synthesis is constrained by the reviewers' dependence on the manuscript material and absence of execution artifacts: because results are presented as single-run point estimates and diagnostic probes are not included, we cannot determine effect size robustness or causal mechanisms with high confidence. We cannot confirm whether discriminator confusion reflects meaningful task-invariance versus underfitting or optimization artifacts, nor whether orthogonality reduces nonlinear semantic redundancy without the requested similarity/MI diagnostics. Assessment of novelty is limited by the reviewers' available literature context: several close precedents exist (domain-adversarial and domain-separation works), so the perceived innovation depends on whether the multi-class + frozen-transfer composition is judged as sufficiently distinct; this judgment remains partially subjective. Finally, conclusions drawn here apply to the reported sentiment/text-classification suite; generalization to other NLP domains or larger-scale tasks cannot be inferred from the present evidence without further experiments.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript describes ASP-MTL: a shared-private LSTM multi-task architecture combining a multi-class task discriminator trained adversarially and a Frobenius-norm orthogonality penalty to reduce contamination and redundancy in shared representations. The authors report single-run error-rate gains across 16 sentiment/text-classification datasets, frozen shared-layer transfer improvements (single- and bi-channel), and illustrative neuron activations suggesting increased specialization under ASP-MTL.
strengths: Clear, implementable architecture that composes multi-class adversarial discrimination, gradient-reversal minimax training, and an orthogonality (Frobenius) penalty into a shared-private LSTM MTL framework (losses formally defined: LAdv, LDiff, L = LTask + λLAdv + γLDiff).

Broad empirical scope: experiments span 16 sentiment/text-classification datasets with per-task tables (Tables 2 and 3) and a systematic frozen shared-layer transfer protocol (single-channel and bi-channel) that operationalizes the 'off-the-shelf' shared extractor idea.
Interpretability effort: neuron-level visualizations (Figure 5) and pattern lists (Table 4) provide qualitative support for claims about reduced contamination and increased specialization.
limitations: Single-run quantitative reporting: Tables 2 and 3 present single point estimates per method/task with no multi-seed averages, standard deviations, or statistical tests; robustness of the reported gains to random initialization and training noise is therefore unknown.

Key mechanistic claims lack direct diagnostics: the central 'purity' claim (that adversarial training makes shared features task-invariant) is not quantified with held-out probe classifiers or discriminator-accuracy-before/after measurements; the orthogonality claim (that the Frobenius penalty enforces semantic disjointness) is supported only by linear decorrelation and anecdotal visualizations, with no nonlinear-similarity or mutual-information analyses.

Baseline parity and tuning transparency: descriptions of competitor implementations (MT-CNN, MT-DNN, FS-MTL, SP-MTL) and their hyperparameter search budgets, parameter counts, and early-stopping/optimizer settings are insufficiently documented to rule out tuning or capacity confounds.

Unvalidated semi-supervised claim and limited transfer regime: although LAdv is said to allow unlabeled-data use, no semi-supervised experiments are provided; transfer experiments evaluate only frozen shared-layer reuse and omit fine-tuning comparisons, limiting practical transfer conclusions.
open_questions: Can the authors provide multi-seed results (recommended ≥5 seeds) with mean ± standard deviation and appropriate paired statistical tests (per-task and average) for the key comparisons (ASP-MTL vs SP-MTL and best baselines) to assess robustness of reported gains?

Do held-out probe classifiers (trained post hoc on frozen shared representations) show reduced task-identifiability after ASP-MTL training? Please report probe accuracy/AUC before and after adversarial training and correlate these measures with transfer/performance gains.

How does LDiff affect nonlinear redundancy between shared and private encodings? Please report one or more nonlinear similarity metrics (e.g., CKA, SVCCA, HSIC, or mutual-information proxies) comparing shared vs private outputs with and without the orthogonality term.

What are the baseline implementation details and tuning protocols? Please provide model parameter counts, embedding handling, optimizer and early-stopping settings, and hyperparameter grids used for all baselines to confirm parity.

How do frozen-transfer and fine-tuned-transfer compare? Please add transfer experiments where the transferred shared layer is fine-tuned on the target and report differences vs frozen transfer (SC/BC) to clarify practical guidance.

What are the minimax training dynamics and stability characteristics (discriminator capacity, λ schedule, gradient-reversal scaling)? Please include training curves (task loss, LAdv, LDiff, discriminator accuracy) and ablations on discriminator architecture and λ/γ sensitivity.
consensus_snapshot: Across reviewers there is agreement that the method is a coherent, implementable composition of known mechanisms (adversarial invariance + orthogonality + shared-private MTL) with plausible empirical benefits demonstrated across many sentiment datasets.

There is consensus that the empirical evaluation is broad (16 datasets, transfer protocol) but that reporting and diagnostic gaps (single-run numbers, lack of held-out probes, limited redundancy metrics, and baseline transparency) materially limit the strength of causal and robustness claims.

All reviewers request multi-seed statistical reporting, direct probes of task-identifiability in shared representations, nonlinear-similarity analyses for redundancy, ablations isolating LAdv vs LDiff, and clearer baseline reproduction details.
disagreement_snapshot: Degree of novelty: some reviewers frame the contribution as an incremental engineering synthesis (combining prior adversarial/domain-separation ideas) while others view the multi-class adversarial + frozen-transfer framing as a modestly interesting compositional innovation. Reviewers differ in how much novelty signal this composition provides given close antecedents (e.g., Bousmalis et al. 2016; Ganin & Lempitsky 2015).

Interpretation of reported gains: some reviewers find the breadth of datasets suggestive that gains are real, pending robustness checks; others emphasize that without multi-seed tests and fair baseline tuning the numerical improvements may reflect tuning or implementation artifacts.

Efficacy of orthogonality: reviewers agree the Frobenius penalty enforces linear decorrelation, but disagree on whether that alone plausibly implies semantic disjointness without nonlinear diagnostic evidence.
uncertainty_snapshot: We cannot determine whether discriminator confusion (if observed) corresponds to useful task-invariance or to underfitting/optimization artifacts without held-out probe results and discriminator-capacity ablations.
We cannot conclude that LDiff achieves semantic disjointness rather than only linear decorrelation without nonlinear-similarity or mutual-information measurements.
We cannot judge the robustness of average error-rate improvements because per-task and across-seed variance is not reported; the magnitude and significance of gains remain uncertain.
We cannot validate the semi-supervised/unlabeled-data claim empirically because no unlabeled-data experiments are included.
source_trace: Manuscript: definitions and equations for adversarial loss LAdv (Eq.13), orthogonality loss LDiff (Eq.14), and total loss L = LTask + λLAdv + γLDiff (Eq.15); cited in shared analysis extracts.
Manuscript empirical artifacts: Table 2 (per-task error rates for 16 datasets, ASP-MTL column) and Table 3 (frozen shared-layer transfer SC/BC results) referenced by multiple reviewers.
Manuscript interpretability artifacts: Figure 5 (neuron activation visualizations) and Table 4 (token/pattern lists) used as qualitative evidence.
Prior work relating to adversarial invariance and minimax optimization: Ganin & Lempitsky (2015) Domain-Adversarial Neural Networks / gradient reversal (cited in manuscript and reviewers' notes).
Prior work relating to shared/private separation and orthogonality penalty: Bousmalis et al. (2016) Domain Separation Networks (cited in manuscript; LDiff resembles their Frobenius-term approach).
Prior theoretical linkage: Ajakan et al. (2014) and domain-adaptation theory connecting adversarial objectives to divergences/H-divergence (manuscript cites these motivations).
transparency_notes: The manuscript provides equation-level definitions and dataset lists (Table 1) and mentions a small hyperparameter grid and embedding initialization (200d GloVe), but omits key reproducibility artifacts: no code link, no random seeds or number-of-runs per result, no full baseline implementation/hyperparameter details or parameter counts, no training curves (losses and discriminator accuracy over epochs), and no held-out probe or redundancy metric computations. These omissions hinder independent verification and mechanistic assessment.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: If authors can run targeted revisions within a reasonable cycle, request that they prioritize: (1) multi-seed reruns (≥5 seeds) and report mean ± std and paired statistical tests for core comparisons (ASP-MTL vs SP-MTL and strongest baselines); (2) held-out probe classifiers (or discriminator-accuracy diagnostics) on frozen shared representations before/after adversarial training to quantify 'purity' and correlate with transfer gains; (3) redundancy analyses using at least one nonlinear similarity metric (e.g., CKA, SVCCA, HSIC, or MI proxy) to assess whether LDiff reduces nonlinear overlap; (4) ablations separating LAdv-only, LDiff-only, and neither conditions across seeds and a sensitivity sweep for λ and γ, plus training curves to document minimax behavior and discriminator capacity choices; and (5) full baseline implementation details and hyperparameter search budgets to ensure fair comparisons. If space/time is constrained, require (1)-(4) and baseline transparency first; the semi-supervised experiment and expanded interpretability statistics are desirable but secondary. Use these diagnostics to re-evaluate claims about mechanisms and robustness.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen claims and address reviewer concerns, provide: (a) multi-seed experimental results (recommended ≥5 seeds) with mean ± std and 95% CIs and paired tests for key comparisons; (b) held-out probe experiments: train independent task-classifiers on frozen shared representations from models trained with/without LAdv and report task-identifiability metrics and their correlation with transfer/performance improvements; (c) redundancy diagnostics: compute CKA/SVCCA/HSIC or mutual-information proxies comparing shared vs private outputs with/without LDiff and report population statistics across tasks and seeds; (d) clear ablations: include LAdv-only, LDiff-only, and full ASP-MTL across multiple seeds and a broader λ/γ sweep, plus training curves (task loss, LAdv, LDiff, discriminator accuracy) and discriminator-capacity ablations to document minimax stability; (e) baseline transparency: release exact baseline architectures, parameter counts, embedding handling, optimizer settings, and hyperparameter grids or cite precise public implementations used; (f) transfer robustness: add experiments comparing frozen vs fine-tuned transferred shared layers (SC/BC) and analyze which target tasks benefit and why (e.g., lexical or domain similarity measures); (g) semi-supervised test (if feasible): include an experiment that injects unlabeled sentences into LAdv to demonstrate the claimed unlabeled-data utility; (h) expand interpretability analyses: report aggregate neuron-specialization statistics (e.g., percent of units whose top-k tokens are unique to shared vs private, activation entropy) rather than only anecdotal examples; and (i) release code, exact dataset splits, and random seeds to facilitate reproducibility. human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The manuscript proposes ASP-MTL: a shared-private LSTM multi-task architecture augmented with a multi-class adversarial task discriminator (minimax via gradient reversal) and a Frobenius-norm orthogonality penalty between shared and private outputs. Experiments on 16 sentiment/text-classification datasets report lower error rates versus single-task and several multi-task baselines; frozen shared-layer transfer (single-channel and bi-channel) is evaluated and illustrative neuron visualizations are provided to support claims of reduced contamination and increased specialization.

Strengths:
- The method is clearly specified (LAdv, LDiff, combined loss) and implementable; it composes complementary, well-motivated mechanisms (adversarial invariance + orthogonality) within a shared-private LSTM framework.
- Empirical breadth is notable: 16 tasks and a systematic frozen-transfer protocol give useful coverage beyond single-dataset studies.
- Authors attempt interpretability via neuron visualizations and pattern extraction to support mechanistic claims.

Limitations:
- Single-run reporting: core numerical results (Tables 2 and 3) lack multi-seed means, variances, and statistical testing, preventing assessment of robustness to initialization and stochastic training.
- Mechanistic diagnostics missing: the 'purity' claim is not directly measured (no held-out probe/discriminator accuracy pre/post), and LDiff is only shown to reduce linear correlations (Frobenius term) without nonlinear-similarity or mutual-information analyses to support semantic disjointness.
- Baseline parity under-documented: competitor implementations, hyperparameter searches, and parameter counts are not fully specified; tuning/capacity confounds cannot be ruled out.
- Semi-supervised/unlabeled claim is untested and transfer experiments examine only frozen reuse (no fine-tuning baseline), limiting practical guidance.

Open Questions:
- Please provide multi-seed (≥5) results with mean ± std and paired statistical tests for ASP-MTL vs SP-MTL and the top baselines (per-task and average). Does significance persist under multiple runs?
- Can you train held-out probe classifiers on frozen shared representations (before/after adversarial training) and report task-identifiability (accuracy/AUC) and its correlation with transfer performance?
- What do nonlinear similarity metrics (CKA/SVCCA/HSIC or MI proxies) show about shared vs private redundancy with and without LDiff? Does orthogonality reduce these measures?
- Please supply full baseline implementation details (architectures, embedding handling, hyperparameter grids, parameter counts) and ensure comparable tuning budgets. Were public baseline implementations used (cite versions)?
- How does frozen transfer compare to fine-tuning the transferred shared layer (SC/BC)? Which target tasks benefit and how does benefit relate to source-target similarity?
- Provide training diagnostics: losses and discriminator accuracy curves, and ablate discriminator capacity and λ/γ sensitivity to demonstrate stability of minimax optimization.

Transparency:
Manuscript includes formal loss definitions and dataset lists, but omits critical reproducibility elements: no code or seeds, no multi-run reporting, limited baseline/tuning disclosure, no held-out probe or redundancy metrics, and no training-curve diagnostics. Providing these artifacts would materially improve verifiability and interpretability.

Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.
